steps.title: What the verb adds to the words
steps.html:
Reporting verbs carry judgement. He said the campaign worked is neutral. He claimed tells the reader the evidence has not been shown. He insisted tells them somebody was arguing back. He admitted tells them the statement cost him something. He denied tells them there was an accusation. Choosing the verb is the main way a reporter shows their reading of a story without giving an opinion.

The patterns matter as much as the meanings. Most take that: argue, claim, insist, point out, announce, indicate, confirm. A group needs a person before that: tell, remind, assure, inform — he assured us that, never he assured that. Admit, deny, report and suggest take -ing or that, and never an infinitive. Promise, refuse, offer, agree, threaten take to + verb. Invite, remind, advise, persuade, ask take a person and then to + verb.

Prepositions. Insist on doing, apologise for doing, accuse somebody of doing, congratulate somebody on doing. The verb after a preposition is always -ing, as in lesson 34.

Backshift still applies. The tense rules from lesson 37 do not change: He admitted that he had taken it. With a present reporting verb, nothing shifts: The company claims the campaign was a success keeps whatever tense was used.

Choosing badly is a real error. He denied that he was late and he admitted that he was late describe two different events; a translator who picks the wrong one has changed the story.

steps.title: The commonest errors at this level
steps.html:
• He denied to take it — deny never takes an infinitive.
  • She suggested to go — suggest takes -ing or that.
  • He assured that it was safe — the person is missing.
  • He insisted to pay — insist on paying.
  • He accused me to steal it — accused me of stealing it.

steps.title: Напиши свой текст
steps.sub: Напиши ответ, затем сверься с образцом
steps.modelHtml:
The city has announced that the bus route through the old market will be closed to traffic from September. Officials say the road is unsafe; two collisions were recorded there last year, and the pavement is one metre wide.

Traders argue that the closure will finish the market. One stallholder pointed out that eighty per cent of his customers arrive by that bus, and that no alternative stop has been announced. The transport department has assured traders that a new stop will open within two hundred metres of the square, but it has not confirmed when. A spokesperson claimed that similar closures elsewhere in the country had increased footfall by a fifth; the figure comes from the department’s own report, and the two towns named in it are both larger than this one.

Not everybody in the market agrees. Three younger traders said they had wanted the road closed for years, and one admitted that she had signed the residents’ petition against her own association. The campaigners deny being funded by the developers who own the corner building, and no evidence has been produced that they are.

What is still unconfirmed is the thing everybody is arguing about: whether the new stop will be in place before the road closes. Until the department answers that, both sides are describing different Septembers.
